query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Switching the feedstock from the standard 15–45 μm powder to a coarser powder (with an extended upper size range) will increase the deposition efficiency and build-up of the FeCoNiCrAl bond coat, thereby attaining the required coating thickness while preserving its integrity and keeping as-sprayed oxidation to a minimum.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy feedstock having a particle size distribution of 15–45 μm, deposited via thermal spraying as a bond coat for TBC systems.
generation.intervention: Replace the existing powder with a coarser feedstock—i.e. a gas-atomized FeCoNiCrAl powder with an extended size distribution (for example, targeting an upper limit beyond 45 μm) while keeping other spray parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Atmospheric plasma spraying (or the established thermal spray method) under identical operational settings (e.g. spray distance, traverse speed, gas composition) and intended service conditions of the bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system.
generation.structural_mediator: The increased particle size raises the in-flight thermal mass, promoting better splat formation and adhesion upon impact, which in turn improves deposition yield and coating build-up; simultaneously, the reduced specific surface area helps limit in-flight oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Larger particles are less prone to complete oxidation due to a lower surface-to-volume ratio and deposit more effectively as they flatten and adhere on impact, thereby increasing the net deposition rate, which overcomes the thickness shortfall without compromising the coating microstructure or oxidation status.
generation.predicted_outcome: The bond coat will achieve a greater thickness relative to the baseline deposition using the 15–45 μm feedstock, with coating integrity maintained and minimal as-sprayed oxidation. The exact magnitude of thickness increase is uncertain and will depend on the new particle size distribution and spray dynamics.
generation.baseline: Coating produced using the standard 15–45 μm feedstock under current thermal spray conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention assumes that other spray parameters (e.g. gas flows, spray distance, power settings) remain constant and that the as-sprayed oxidation remains minimal as previously observed.
generation.uncertainty: The precise gain in deposition thickness is not predicted numerically, as it depends on the specifics of the new powder size distribution and potential shifts in particle thermal histories; further optimization might be required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeCoNiCrAl bond coats by thermal spray deposition under identical conditions on identical substrates: one set using the baseline 15–45 μm powder and another using the coarser powder with an extended upper size limit. Ensure that all other process parameters (spray distance, gas flows, power, and traverse speed) remain the same. After deposition, cross-section the coatings and measure the overall coating thickness, assess the microstructure, and quantify any oxidation features using SEM and XRD.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings deposited with the coarser powder do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in thickness compared to the baseline or if they show higher levels of in-flight oxidation or degraded microstructural integrity, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, the powder milled for 10 h was chosen as a feedstock to deposit the coating by atmospheric plasma spraying. Prior to spraying, the feedstock powder was dried in an oven at 200 °C for 3 h to remove the moisture and improve its flowability. First, 316 stainless steel cylindrical specimens with dimensions of Φ 25 × 7 mm were used as substrates. Before spraying, the substrates were cleaned with an ultrasonic cleaner in acetone for 10 min, and then dried with a dryer. To improve the bonding strength of the coating, sand blasting one side of the substrate was carried out to obtain a certain cleanliness and roughness. During sand blasting, an Al2O3 particle with a size of less than 1.25 mm was used as an abrasive. The substrates were sandblasted under a compressed air pressure of about 0.5 MPa for 30 s. An APS system (3710, PRAXAIR SURFACE TECHNOLOGIES, Indianapolis, IN, USA) with a high-energy plasma gun (SG-100) was employed to deposit the coating. During spraying, argon was used as a primary gas, and nitrogen was used as a secondary gas, whose pressures were 0.4 and 0.3 MPa, respectively.
